title: Chemical Bonding
tagline: Learn how atoms combine through electron transfer and sharing to form stable compounds.

overview.intro: Chemical bonding explains why and how atoms combine to achieve stable electronic configurations. In ICSE Class 10, emphasis is placed on electrovalent (ionic) bonding formed by transfer of electrons and covalent bonding formed by sharing of electrons, along with coordinate bonding as a special case of sharing. Understanding electron-dot structures, properties of ionic and covalent compounds, and conditions favouring bond formation helps students predict compound behaviour and answer reasoning questions accurately.

facts.label: Covalent bond
facts.value: Sharing of electron pairs between atoms

learningOutcomes: Explain the cause of chemical bonding in terms of stability and electronic configuration.
Describe formation of electrovalent bonds with electron-dot structures.
Describe formation of covalent and coordinate bonds with suitable examples.
Compare properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
Identify bond type from given elements or compound properties.

learn.title: Stability and Cause of Chemical Combination

blocks.text: Atoms combine because most isolated atoms do not have a completely filled outermost shell and are therefore less stable. By losing, gaining or sharing electrons, atoms tend to attain the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas, which is associated with stability.

The nature of the bond formed depends on the electronegativity difference and the tendency of participating atoms to lose or gain electrons. Metals usually lose electrons, non-metals usually gain or share electrons, and these tendencies determine whether bonding is ionic or covalent.

items: Stable configuration generally means a complete valence shell.
Bond formation is accompanied by a decrease in potential energy of the system.
The number of valence electrons governs valency and bonding capacity.
Electron-dot (Lewis) symbols represent valence electrons around atomic symbols.

blocks.text: An electrovalent bond is formed by complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metallic atom to a non-metallic atom. The metal becomes a positively charged cation and the non-metal becomes a negatively charged anion; the oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces.

Formation of sodium chloride is a classic example: sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to form Na+, while chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to form Cl−. Both attain stable configurations, and the ionic lattice is held by attraction between ions.

items.text: Na → Na+ + e− and Cl + e− → Cl−; ions combine to form NaCl.
items.note: Electron transfer produces oppositely charged ions.

items.text: MgCl2 formation involves Mg losing two electrons to two chlorine atoms.
items.note: Total electrons lost equal total electrons gained.

blocks.text: A covalent bond is formed by mutual sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between atoms, usually non-metals. Each shared pair constitutes one covalent bond. By sharing, the participating atoms attain stable valence configurations without forming ions.

Single, double and triple covalent bonds involve sharing of one, two and three pairs of electrons respectively. Examples include H2 and Cl2 (single), O2 (double) and N2 (triple). Electron-dot structures show shared pairs between atoms and lone pairs on individual atoms.

items: Covalent bonds are directional and form molecules.
Shared electrons are counted in the valence shell of both atoms.
Non-polar covalent bonds occur between similar atoms; polar covalent bonds occur when sharing is unequal.
Molecular formulae and electron-dot diagrams must show correct valency and shared pairs.

blocks.text: A coordinate bond is a type of covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are contributed by the same atom (donor) to another atom or ion (acceptor) that has a vacant orbital. Once formed, it behaves like an ordinary covalent bond in the resulting species.

Common examples at this level include formation of the ammonium ion, NH4+, where the lone pair on nitrogen in ammonia is donated to H+, and formation of the hydronium ion, H3O+, where water donates a lone pair to H+. Electron-dot structures help identify the donor lone pair.

items.meaning: The atom that provides both electrons for the shared pair in a coordinate bond.
The atom or ion with a vacant orbital that receives the shared pair.
A pair of valence electrons not involved in bonding but available for donation.

learn.title: Properties of Ionic and Covalent Compounds

blocks.text: Ionic compounds consist of ions arranged in a lattice and generally have high melting and boiling points, are hard and brittle, conduct electricity in molten state or aqueous solution, and are often soluble in water. Covalent compounds consist of molecules and generally have lower melting and boiling points, do not conduct electricity in solution (except those that ionise), and are often soluble in organic solvents.

These differences arise from the nature of particles and forces: strong electrostatic forces in ionic lattices versus weaker intermolecular forces in many covalent molecular substances. When comparing compounds, refer to particle type, force, and mobility of ions or electrons.

keyPoints: Atoms bond to attain stable electronic configurations, usually like noble gases.
Electrovalent bonds form by complete transfer of electrons between metal and non-metal.
Covalent bonds form by sharing of electron pairs, usually between non-metals.
Coordinate bonds involve donation of a lone pair by one atom to an acceptor.
Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct electricity when ions are mobile.
Covalent molecular compounds usually have low melting points and poor electrical conduction.
Electron-dot structures must show correct valence electrons and shared/transferred electrons.
Single, double and triple bonds correspond to one, two and three shared pairs.
Bond type depends on the nature of combining atoms and electron behaviour.
Properties of compounds are explained by particles present and forces between them.
examFocus: Draw and interpret electron-dot structures for ionic and covalent compounds.
Explain ionic bond formation with electron transfer and resulting ions.
Distinguish ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds with clear definitions and examples.
Compare properties of ionic and covalent compounds with reasons.
Identify donor and acceptor in coordinate bond examples like NH4+ and H3O+.
Balance electron loss and gain in ionic bond equations/diagrams.
Use correct terms: cation, anion, lone pair, shared pair, electrostatic attraction.

vocabulary.meaning: A bond formed by complete transfer of electrons and attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A bond formed by mutual sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between atoms.
A covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by the same atom.
A positively charged ion formed by loss of electrons.
A negatively charged ion formed by gain of electrons.
Electrons in the outermost shell involved in bonding.
A pair of valence electrons not shared in a bond.
A diagram showing valence electrons as dots around atomic symbols.
A covalent bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons.
A covalent bond formed by sharing two pairs of electrons.
Force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

questions.prompt: An electrovalent bond is formed by:
questions.answer: transfer of electrons
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding involves complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse electron transfer with sharing.

questions.prompt: A covalent bond is formed by:
questions.answer: mutual sharing of electron pairs
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding occurs when atoms share valence electrons to attain stability.
questions.commonMistake: Sharing involves electron pairs, not proton transfer.

questions.prompt: In the formation of NaCl, sodium becomes:
questions.answer: Na+ by losing an electron
questions.explanation: Sodium loses its one valence electron to achieve a stable configuration and forms a cation.
questions.commonMistake: Metals form positive ions by electron loss.

questions.prompt: Which compound is expected to conduct electricity in aqueous solution?
questions.answer: Sodium chloride
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds produce mobile ions in water, allowing electrical conduction.
questions.commonMistake: Covalent molecular substances generally do not form ions in water.

questions.prompt: A coordinate bond is formed when:
options: both electrons are donated by one atom
questions.answer: both electrons are donated by one atom
questions.explanation: In a coordinate bond, a donor provides a lone pair to an acceptor.
questions.commonMistake: After formation it is shown as a shared pair, but origin differs.

questions.prompt: The bond in an oxygen molecule (O2) involves sharing of:
questions.answer: two pairs of electrons
questions.explanation: O2 has a double covalent bond formed by sharing two electron pairs.
questions.commonMistake: Count shared pairs to identify single, double or triple bonds.

questions.prompt: Which property is typical of covalent molecular compounds?
questions.answer: Low melting and boiling points
questions.explanation: Weak intermolecular forces in many covalent molecules lead to lower melting and boiling points.
questions.commonMistake: Do not attribute ionic lattice properties to molecular covalent substances.

questions.prompt: In the formation of NH4+, the donor atom is:
questions.answer: nitrogen in ammonia
questions.explanation: Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+ to form the coordinate bond in ammonium ion.
questions.commonMistake: The acceptor H+ has no electrons to donate.

questions.prompt: A negatively charged ion is called an ________.
questions.answer: anion
questions.explanation: An anion is formed when an atom gains electrons.
questions.commonMistake: Cations are positively charged ions.

questions.prompt: A pair of electrons shared between two atoms forms a ________ bond.
questions.answer: covalent
questions.explanation: Sharing of electron pairs constitutes covalent bonding.
questions.commonMistake: Transfer of electrons forms an electrovalent bond.

questions.prompt: The pair of valence electrons not involved in bonding is called a ________ pair.
questions.answer: lone
questions.explanation: Lone pairs may remain on an atom or be donated in coordinate bonding.
questions.commonMistake: Shared pairs participate in covalent bonds.

questions.prompt: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?
questions.answer: Atoms form chemical bonds to attain more stable electronic configurations, usually by completing their outermost shells like noble gases. Bond formation lowers the energy of the system.
questions.explanation: Stability through valence-shell completion is the main driving factor.
questions.commonMistake: Mention stability or noble-gas configuration in your answer.

questions.prompt: Explain the formation of an electrovalent bond between sodium and chlorine.
questions.answer: Sodium loses one valence electron to form Na+, and chlorine gains that electron to form Cl−. The resulting oppositely charged ions attract each other by electrostatic force, forming sodium chloride.
questions.explanation: Electron transfer and ionic attraction are both essential parts of the explanation.
questions.commonMistake: State which atom loses and which gains electrons.

questions.prompt: What is a coordinate bond? Give one example.
questions.answer: A coordinate bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom to another atom or ion. For example, in NH4+, nitrogen in ammonia donates a lone pair to H+ to form a coordinate bond.
questions.explanation: The example should clearly identify the donor lone pair and acceptor.
questions.commonMistake: Do not describe it as transfer of electrons to form separate ions.

questions.prompt: State three differences between ionic and covalent compounds.
questions.answer: Ionic compounds are made of ions, usually have high melting and boiling points, and conduct electricity in molten or aqueous state. Covalent molecular compounds are made of molecules, usually have lower melting and boiling points, and generally do not conduct electricity.
questions.explanation: Differences should relate to particles, forces and observable properties.
questions.commonMistake: Give paired comparisons rather than unrelated properties.

questions.prompt: Describe the formation of a covalent bond in nitrogen molecule with the help of electron sharing concept.
questions.answer: A nitrogen atom has five valence electrons and needs three more to complete its octet. In N2, each nitrogen atom shares three electrons with the other, forming three shared pairs or a triple covalent bond. Each atom also retains one lone pair. By sharing six electrons in total, both nitrogen atoms attain stable configurations.
questions.explanation: The answer should state valence electrons, shared pairs and lone pairs.
questions.commonMistake: N2 has a triple bond, not a single or double bond.

questions.prompt: Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity in molten state but not in solid state.
questions.answer: In solid ionic compounds, ions are held in fixed positions within a rigid lattice and cannot move freely, so they do not conduct electricity. In molten state, the lattice breaks down and ions become mobile. These free-moving ions carry charge through the liquid, enabling electrical conduction.
questions.explanation: Electrical conduction in ionic substances requires mobility of charged particles.
questions.commonMistake: Mention ions, not electrons, as charge carriers in ionic compounds.

questions.prompt: Compare electrovalent and covalent bonds on the basis of formation, particles, and two properties of their compounds.
questions.answer: Electrovalent bonds form by complete transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal, producing ions held by electrostatic attraction; covalent bonds form by mutual sharing of electron pairs between atoms, producing molecules. Ionic compounds generally have high melting points and conduct electricity in molten or aqueous state due to mobile ions. Covalent molecular compounds generally have low melting and boiling points and poor electrical conduction because they consist of neutral molecules with weaker intermolecular forces.
questions.explanation: A good comparison links bond formation to particle type and resulting properties.
questions.commonMistake: Cover all parts asked: formation, particles and properties.

questions.prompt: Element X (2,8,1) combines with element Y (2,8,7). Predict the type of bond formed and describe the process.
questions.answer: X will lose one electron to form X+ and Y will gain one electron to form Y−, both attaining stable configurations. The oppositely charged ions attract each other, so an electrovalent (ionic) bond is formed.
questions.explanation: Electronic configurations indicate metal-like electron loss and non-metal-like electron gain.
questions.commonMistake: Show the direction of electron transfer clearly.

questions.prompt: Carbon tetrachloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Explain this observation.
questions.answer: Carbon tetrachloride is a covalent molecular compound with no free ions or electrons to carry charge, so it does not conduct electricity. Molten sodium chloride contains mobile Na+ and Cl− ions released from the lattice, which move under an electric field and conduct electricity.
questions.explanation: The explanation must focus on presence or absence of mobile charged particles.
questions.commonMistake: Do not state that all liquids conduct electricity.

questions.prompt: Ammonia reacts with hydrogen ion to form ammonium ion. Identify the type of bond formed between N and the added H+, and justify using electron-dot concept.
questions.answer: A coordinate bond is formed between nitrogen in ammonia and the added H+. Nitrogen has a lone pair in NH3, while H+ has no electrons but can accept a pair. Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+, creating a shared pair in NH4+; once formed, this bond is equivalent to the other N–H bonds in the ion.
questions.explanation: Justification should mention donor lone pair and acceptor vacancy.
questions.commonMistake: The bond is coordinate in origin, not an ionic bond.

questions.prompt: Two elements A and B both need one electron to complete their octets. Predict the likely bond type between them and justify.
questions.answer: A and B are likely to form a covalent bond by sharing one pair of electrons, so that each attains a stable octet. Since both need electrons rather than readily losing them, transfer is unlikely and mutual sharing is favoured.
questions.explanation: The prediction follows from the electron requirement of both atoms.
questions.commonMistake: Consider whether either atom is a typical electron donor metal before predicting ionic bonding.
